documents: Chen et al. 2022, Acta Geologica Sinica (English Edition) 96(5): 1764-1777, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: At present, the formation processes of tafoni and honeycombs remain controversial.

steps.action: The authors state that the formation processes of tafoni and honeycombs are unresolved in the literature.
steps.quote: At present, the formation processes of tafoni and honeycombs remain controversial.

steps.action: The authors list published candidate agents: salt weathering, organisms, internal moisture, case-hardening and core softening, wetting-drying cycles, thermal stress, slope aspect and self-organization.
steps.quote: Salt weathering has been often thought to be a key factor

steps.action: The authors add Bruthans et al.'s view that organizing factors (hydraulic field, stress, boundary conditions) matter more than decay agents.
steps.quote: Bruthans et al. (2018) suggested that too much emphasis has been given to these different weathering agents

steps.action: The authors set two aims: describe the honeycombs, tafoni and case-hardening on all slopes, and assess the weathering agents and formation processes.
steps.quote: (2) to assess the weathering agents and formation processes of cavernous forms.

steps.action: The authors choose the Yongningshan hill, with caverns on all four slope aspects, as a found setting for assessing cavern development.
steps.quote: this special environment provides a good opportunity to assess cavern development and rock decay mechanisms

steps.action: A March 2019 field survey describes and measures the cavernous forms, salt efflorescence and case-hardening slope by slope (methods p. 1765; results pp. 1766-1771).
steps.quote: both cavernous features and case-hardening are much more massively developed on the western slope.

steps.action: Thin-section and SEM/EDX observation characterizes grain size, composition, cements, dissolution features and salt crystals on grains.
steps.quote: the great bulk of detrital grains are mainly fine- to medium-grained

steps.action: Schmidt hammer rebound values are recorded at 36 sites on niches, columns and outer surfaces of the four slopes.
steps.quote: In total, 720 SH rebound values were obtained at 36 sites

steps.action: Niche and column hardness are compared; lower niche values are read as case-hardening of outer surfaces, and the southern-slope exception is attributed to intense salt weathering.
steps.quote: the mean value within niches is less than that measured at the column or head

steps.action: Electrical conductivity and cation and anion contents of leachates from niche, column and surface samples are measured (ICP-OES, ion chromatography).
steps.quote: the interiors are more saline and moist than the intervening heads

steps.action: The dominant salt minerals are inferred from the ion contents, without direct mineral identification.
steps.quote: salts dominant in the weathering processes are probably composed of gypsum, potassium nitrate, sodium nitrate

steps.action: Major oxides are measured by XRF and compared with average continental crust composition.
steps.quote: all tested samples are characterized by higher SiO2 and lower Al2O3, CaO, K2O and Na2O contents

steps.action: Head and niche samples are compared for Fe, Mn, conductivity and hardness, and the authors infer salt accumulation in sheltered interiors.
steps.quote: suggesting that soluble salts have accumulated within the interiors

steps.action: The authors take from Huinink et al.'s physical model the expectation that drying-period length controls tafoni growth.
steps.quote: the length of the drying period is considered a crucial parameter for the growth of tafoni

steps.action: Local precipitation and evaporation data are compared with that expectation, showing long dry and short wet periods that favour salt accumulation.
steps.quote: featuring a long dry period and a short wet period in a single year

steps.action: Wind-blown loess from northerly dust storms, seepage, rain and capillary rise are proposed as suppliers of moisture and salts.
steps.quote: seepage water from the caprock, rains, capillary wicking from groundwater and wind-blown loess all provide both moisture and salts

steps.action: The aspect-dependent salt and cavern pattern (insolation and evaporation by slope) is compared with weathering patterns reported at Petra.
steps.quote: These findings are consistent with weathering patterns found in Petra, Jordan (Paradise, 2013b).

steps.action: Water vapour from the Luohe River at the concave western bank is proposed to explain the western slope's extra cavern and crust development.
steps.quote: also related to an accessible supply of water vapour from the Luohe River

steps.action: Salt weathering is corroborated by two methods: salt crystals in SEM images and water-soluble salt chemistry.
steps.quote: salt weathering is also confirmed by the development of salt crystals on the silicate mineral grains in SEM images and salt chemistry experiments

steps.action: Two salt sources are proposed, the Cretaceous desert sandstone itself and wind-blown dust, without discriminating between them.
steps.quote: The salts have two possible sources.

steps.action: Crust penetration, breakage at weak points and second-generation tafoni in hardened interiors are compared, and the authors infer a genetic link between case-hardening and cavern development.
steps.quote: These observations collectively indicate a genetic relationship between cavern development and case-hardening.

steps.action: The moisture regime (attenuated temperatures, higher humidity in hollows) is proposed as a further possible agent.
steps.quote: The moisture regime could be another potential agent responsible for cavern development

steps.action: The authors keep a polygenetic account: porous aeolian sandstone lithology is fundamental, and wetting-drying, aeolian salt, moisture and river vapour are key factors.
steps.quote: The aeolian sandstones of the Luohe Formation are fundamental for the development of cavernous weathering forms

tree.answer: Cavernous weathering (honeycombs, tafoni, case-hardening) differing across four slopes of the YNS hill
Forms, salts and hardness observed directly; formation processes not, inferred from traces
Describe the forms and assess weathering agents and formation processes
Agents listed from the literature (salt, moisture, case-hardening, lithology, organizing factors), not set as competing rivals
No distinct predictions derived for the rivals
Conditions found: one hill, four slope aspects, one field campaign

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: four slope aspects act as natural variation in insolation and moisture
Partly: salt presence corroborated by SEM and salt chemistry; no sensitivity or replication tests
Polygenetic best explanation centred on lithology and salt weathering

end.claim: Cavernous weathering at YNS develops in porous, permeable aeolian Luohe sandstones under long dry periods, aeolian salts and moisture; the western slope's massive caverns and crusts are probably related to dust-borne salts and water vapour from the Luohe River.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing salt chemistry, conductivity and hardness between niche and head samples is what grounds the claim that salts accumulate in sheltered interiors and drive cavern growth.

gates.evidence: Salt chemistry sampling followed Goudie et al. (2002a), reflecting the prior salt-weathering view (p. 1766). Salt measurements could in principle have shown little salt, but no rival was given a prediction that could fail (pp. 1773, 1775). Nothing is reported as fixed before data collection.

imports.item: ICP-OES, ion chromatography and conductivity meter for leachate chemistry
Huinink et al. (2004) physical model of tafoni growth with drying-period length as control parameter
semiconducting metal-oxide coatings converting sunlight and nourishing microorganisms (Lu et al. 2014)

novelty_claims.quote: [...] , provides an example of quantitative experimental study on the cavernous weathering of sandstone landforms in the Loess Plateau.
cavernous weathering phenomena within cliff walls have received little attention, particularly in quantitative experimental studies.

limits: Single field campaign (late March 2019) and uneven sampling (only 2 Schmidt hammer sites on the southern slope); no replicate analyses or uncertainties reported for the chemistry. Salt minerals are inferred from ion contents, not identified by XRD (sub-claim: estimate without stated resolution). No in-situ moisture, temperature or evaporation measurements; the moisture-regime and Luohe-River-vapour explanations are proposed ('possibly', 'probably'), not tested (sub-claims at hypothesis level, not best_explanation). The two salt sources are not discriminated. Agents from the literature are not turned into rivals with distinct predictions, so no rival is excluded. Inference: trace_series fits only loosely, because the four slopes stand in for repetition without a controlled comparison. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown beyond the thanks to anonymous reviewers.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Salts derived both from the Cretaceous aeolian sandstones and from wind-blown dust
alternatives_considered.reason: arid desert depositional environment of the sandstone; frequent northerly dust storms in winter and spring
